corpus_definition: Recorded on a digital disc or video format.
usage_note: on + CD / DVD / video, after have, buy, watch, come out, be available: 'I have the film on DVD.' 'Her new album is out on CD.' No article: say 'on DVD', not 'on a DVD', when you mean the format.

relations.note: Related: saved so you can watch or listen again later; it does not say which format.
Related: recorded on cassette tape, an older format.
Happening now in front of people, not recorded.

context.text: I don't have that film on DVD, but my uncle has all his old concerts on video. Today most people stream music instead of buying it on CD.

reviewer_note: Headword covers three formats; the usage note explains there is no article before the format name.

corpus_definition: Doing something because you wanted to, not by mistake.
usage_note: verb + (object) + on purpose, usually at the end of the clause: 'He broke it on purpose.' Very common in the negative: 'I didn't do it on purpose!'

relations.note: Same meaning; a little more formal.
Same meaning; more formal, used in writing.
Same meaning, but less common than on purpose.
It happened without anyone planning it.
You did it because you made an error.
Without wanting or planning to.

context.text: My little sister dropped my phone, but she didn't do it on purpose. I think the cat pushed the cup off the table on purpose, though!

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; no forms. Purpose itself is a separate noun entry.

corpus_definition: Happening exactly at the planned or expected time.
usage_note: be / arrive / finish + on schedule: 'The project is on schedule.' Compare 'ahead of schedule' (earlier than planned) and 'behind schedule' (later than planned).

relations.note: Same meaning and more common in everyday English.
Close: in the way that was planned, not only at the right time.
Formal; used about people and transport arriving at the exact time.
Later than planned.
After the expected time.

context.text: The new metro line in Tashkent is on schedule and will open in spring. Our train to Samarkand also left exactly on schedule this morning.

reviewer_note: Fixed phrase; ahead of / behind schedule mentioned in the usage note as related patterns.

corpus_definition: The raised floor where people perform in a theater.
usage_note: be / go / walk / appear + on stage: 'She went on stage at eight.' Also written as one word, onstage. British spelling: theatre.

relations.note: Same meaning, written as one word.
Related: singing, acting or dancing for an audience, not only in a theater.
Not on the stage, where the audience cannot see.
In the area behind the stage, where performers get ready.

context.text: When the singer walked on stage, everyone started to clap. She was nervous before the show, but on stage she looked calm and happy.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the definition describes the noun stage, not the phrase on stage (= performing on the stage); map follows the phrase use shown in the example.

corpus_definition: The person you are playing or fighting against in a contest.

forms.definition: a person you play, compete or argue against
forms.example: My opponent played a very good game of chess.
forms.note: Also a person who disagrees with an idea or plan: 'opponents of the new law'.

syn.note: Close; a rival competes with you often or for a long time.
Close; used for sport and business, a little more formal.
Related: a person who tries to win against the champion.
Much stronger: an enemy hates you or fights you in a war.

ant.note: A person who plays on the same team as you.
A person or country that helps and supports you.

forms.definition: the person or team you are competing against
forms.example: Our team was strong, but the opposition was even stronger.
forms.note: Usually 'the opposition'. Also means disagreeing with a plan: 'opposition to the new road'.

syn.note: 'The competition' also means the people you are trying to win against.

forms.definition: to compete or fight against someone; to disagree with a plan
forms.example: Uzbekistan will oppose Japan in the final.
forms.note: In everyday English this verb is most often about disagreeing: 'Many people opposed the plan.'

syn.note: Easy, everyday way to say it about sport and games.
Close; used for sport and business.
Related: try to beat someone, often with force.

ant.note: Help or agree with someone or something.

forms.definition: playing, competing or fighting against you
forms.example: The opposing team scored in the last minute.

syn.note: Same meaning before a noun: 'the rival team'.
Close; often used for companies or ideas.

forms.definition: completely different; or on the other side, facing something
forms.note: Belongs to the 'facing / completely different' meaning of the family, not a person you play against. A very common word.

forms.definition: on the other side of a street or room, facing you
forms.example: The family who live opposite are very friendly.
forms.note: Belongs to the 'facing' meaning of the family, not a person you play against.

context.text: In the final, Dilnoza played against a strong opponent from Kazakhstan. The opposing team's fans were very loud, but she stayed calm and won the match.

reviewer_note: Two rows merged (game/fight and game/argument are one meaning); lowest CEFR B1. Opponent is a person noun headword, so it stays the main noun entry; opposite shown as other_meaning (facing / completely different).

corpus_definition: A choice that you can make.

forms.definition: one of the things you can choose from
forms.example: We have another option if this plan fails.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common.
Close; another thing you can choose instead of the first one.
Related: something that might happen or that you could do.

forms.definition: to choose one thing instead of another
forms.example: Most students opt for English as their second language.
forms.note: Usually 'opt for something' or 'opt to do something'. Also 'opt out (of)' = choose not to take part.

syn.note: Same meaning; choose is the everyday word.
Close; more formal, often about choosing carefully from many.
Related: make up your mind; opt always means choosing between things.

ant.note: Say no to something you are offered.

forms.definition: that you can choose to do or have, but do not have to
forms.example: Art is an optional subject at our school.

syn.note: Close; done because you want to, not because you must.
Related: used for school or university subjects, mainly American English.

ant.note: You must do it; it is a rule.

forms.definition: if you choose to, but you do not have to
forms.example: Serve the soup hot, optionally with fresh bread.
forms.note: Not very common; often seen in recipes and instructions.

syn.note: Related: because you want to, not because you must.

context.text: At our school in Namangan, music is optional. Most students opt for extra English or IT lessons, because they think those are the best options for the future.

reviewer_note: Opt is a separate entry but shares the root with option/optional; optimal and optimist are a different root (best) and are left out.

corpus_definition: Not special, different, or strange; quite normal.

forms.definition: the quality of being normal and not special
forms.example: I love the ordinariness of a quiet Sunday at home.
forms.note: Not very common; usually in writing.

syn.note: Close; a normal situation. American English also says normalcy.

forms.definition: normal and usual, not special or different
forms.example: It was just an ordinary day at work.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common.
Close; what happens most of the time.
Close; used before a noun: 'everyday life'.
Close; something you see or find often.
Close; typical of most people or things.
Related: showing what a group is usually like.

ant.note: Better or more important than usual.
Very unusual and surprising, often in a good way.

forms.example: Ordinarily, I take the bus, but today I walked.

syn.note: Same meaning and more common.
Same meaning and more common.
Close; in most cases.

context.text: It was an ordinary Monday in Andijan. Ordinarily, Bobur takes the bus to work, but today the sun was shining, so he walked.

reviewer_note: Extraordinary is an opposite (in the ant list), not a family form.

corpus_definition: When a machine is broken and not working.
usage_note: be + out of order, after the noun, often on signs for public machines: 'The lift is out of order.' (American English: elevator.) In informal British English it can also mean 'behaving badly': 'That comment was out of order.'

relations.note: Same meaning; broken can be used before a noun too: 'a broken phone'.
Easy, everyday way to say it.
Close; has a problem that stops it working well.
Doing its job correctly.

context.text: The ATM near our flat is out of order again, so I had to walk to the bank. The coffee machine at work was out of order too!

reviewer_note: Map keeps the machine meaning; the British 'behaving badly' meaning is only mentioned in the usage note.

corpus_definition: during or for the whole night; happening very quickly or suddenly

forms.note: No common noun in this family.
No verb in learner use. American English sometimes uses this word as a verb (= stay one night), but it is rare; say 'stay the night'.

forms.definition: happening during the night, or for one night
forms.example: We took the overnight train to Khiva.
forms.note: Used before a noun: 'an overnight bus', 'an overnight stay'.

syn.note: Close; lasting the whole night: 'an all-night party'.

forms.definition: during the night, or for the whole night
forms.example: Leave the beans in water overnight.

syn.note: Close; for the whole night.
Close; from evening until morning.

context.text: We took the overnight bus from Tashkent to Termez. We slept on the bus, so we didn't need to stay overnight in a hotel.

reviewer_note: One corpus row with two meanings, split into two maps (Night, Suddenly), as with boom and commission. Over- + night is a compound, so no affix is claimed. Verb use (mainly US 'we overnighted in...') is rare and not in the gate dictionary, so the verb slot is no_form with a note.

corpus_definition: during or for the whole night; happening very quickly or suddenly

forms.note: No common noun in this family.
No verb in learner use. American English sometimes uses this word as a verb (= stay one night), but it is rare; say 'stay the night'.

forms.definition: happening very quickly and without warning
forms.example: The film was an overnight success.
forms.note: Used before a noun: 'an overnight success', 'an overnight star'.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common.
Close; happening immediately.
Related: very fast, but not always unexpected.

forms.example: The town became famous almost overnight after the news.

syn.note: Same meaning and very common.
Close; immediately, with no time at all.
Related: fast, but not always unexpected.

context.text: Madina's cooking video got a million views overnight. She became an overnight star, and her life changed very quickly.

reviewer_note: Second map for the 'suddenly' meaning; the corpus example uses this one.

corpus_definition: To have an obligation to give money back to someone.

forms.note: No noun in this family. For the money you have to pay back, use 'debt' (a different word).

forms.definition: to have to pay back money that someone lent you
forms.example: I owe my friend ten dollars.
forms.note: Also 'owe someone a favour' and 'owe something to someone' (= have it because of them): other uses of the same verb.

syn.note: Close; 'be in debt to someone' is more formal and usually about larger amounts.
Related: easy words for the same idea, but not only for borrowed money.

forms.example: There is still fifty dollars owing on the bill.
forms.note: Used after the noun, mainly in British English. Don't confuse with 'owing to' (= because of).

syn.note: Same meaning and easier.
Formal: not yet paid or done.
Related: must be paid now or by a certain date.

ant.note: The money has been given back.

context.text: Jasur owes his brother 200,000 som. He paid half of it last week, so 100,000 som is still owing.

reviewer_note: Owner looks similar but comes from own, not owe (people_not_family). Owing to = because of is a false friend, noted on owing.
